question: What problem does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) solve, according to the course material?
reference_answer: The semantic-search course material explains that LLMs generate fluent text but cannot reliably access specific facts because their knowledge is frozen at training time and they sometimes hallucinate. RAG addresses this by dynamically retrieving relevant documents at inference time and injecting them into the LLM's prompt as context, grounding the model's answers in retrieved facts to reduce hallucination.
notes: Grounded in the RAG section of semantic_search.html; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: How does the course material summarize what semantic search is and how bi-encoders differ from cross-encoders?
reference_answer: The course material's summary defines semantic search as 'embeddings + nearest-neighbor search': a bi-encoder encodes the query and document separately into a shared vector space and retrieves the closest vectors, while a cross-encoder concatenates both into a single sequence and produces one relevance score with full cross-attention -- far more accurate but too slow for first-stage retrieval, so the two are typically combined in a two-stage pipeline (optionally adding an LLM at the end for RAG).
expected_sources: semantic_search.html, section 09 Summary & Quick-Start Model Reference
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in the summary section of semantic_search.html; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: What perspective does the lecture material offer on why Transformers need a Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer?
reference_answer: The lecture material explains that FFN layers can be viewed as key-value memories: the first linear layer (768->3072) produces 3072 activation patterns that each match a learned input pattern, and the second linear layer (3072->768) maps those matches back to output representations -- so each of the 3072 intermediate neurons effectively stores a learned fact or transformation rule.
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in slide 54 of the Transformer Architectures & BERT deck; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: How does the GPT lecture material define the temperature and top_p sampling parameters?
reference_answer: According to the GPT lecture slides, temperature (default 1.0, range 0.0-100.0) controls the randomness of sampling -- 1 means regular sampling, 0 always takes the highest-scoring token (more confident, less random), and values approaching 100 push the distribution closer to uniform (less confident, more random). top_p is a float defining which tokens fall within the sampling operation by cumulative probability, while top_k is an integer capping how many top tokens are considered (set to 0 to deactivate).
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in slide 52 of the GPT deck; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: Why does the optimization lecture material say tokenization especially matters for Turkish?
reference_answer: The lecture material explains that tokenization is not cosmetic -- every wasted token is wasted compute at training time and wasted KV-cache at inference -- and that the relevant metric is 'fertility' (average tokens per word). For agglutinative languages like Turkish, where a single word such as 'evlerimizdekilerden' can carry the meaning of an entire English clause ('from the ones in our houses'), fertility differences across tokenizers become large; the material reports that in the group's Turkish LM scaling work (60M-11B parameters), SPM Unigram achieved the best fertility.
expected_sources: 01_architectures.html, section 7.1 Tokenizer Fertility: Why Turkish Hurts
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in section 7.1 of 01_architectures.html; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: How does the GPT lecture material distinguish zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot learning?
reference_answer: The slides describe all three as machine-learning approaches for scenarios with limited or no training examples: zero-shot learning is when a model recognizes/classifies tasks it never saw during training; one-shot learning is recognizing a class from just one training example; and few-shot learning is training with a small number of examples per class.
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in slide 62 of the GPT deck (same wording also appears in the Prompt Engineering deck slide 13); verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: According to the Semantic Search & RAG lecture, what makes a cross-encoder different from a bi-encoder when reranking results?
reference_answer: The lecture explains that, unlike a bi-encoder which encodes the query and document independently, a cross-encoder takes the query and document as a single combined input and produces one scalar relevance score -- letting the model see both texts simultaneously and capture interactions between every query token and every document token. This makes cross-encoders more accurate for reranking but too slow to use as the first-stage retriever over a whole corpus.
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in page 9 ('03 Reranking -- Cross-Encoders') of the Semantic Search & RAG PDF; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: What is the scaled dot-product self-attention formula given in the BERT lecture handout, and how does BERT use multiple attention heads?
reference_answer: The BERT lecture handout gives the formula Output = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) . V for scaled dot-product attention, then explains multi-head attention: instead of one attention function, BERT splits the computation into multiple parallel heads (projecting the input into 12 separate Q, K, V sets, each in a 64-dimensional subspace), so the model can capture different types of relationships simultaneously before the heads are concatenated back together.
notes: Near-verbatim grounding (formula + 12-head / 64-dim description) in the BERT lecture handout; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.

question: Why does the optimization lecture material say the KV cache matters for serving large language models?
reference_answer: The material frames the KV cache as central to LLM inference efficiency -- it revisits the cache 'met in Lecture 1' to quantify its exact size and how that constrains real systems, discusses why the decode phase is memory-bound (the 'roofline argument'), and devotes whole sections to the cache's size formula and to PagedAttention/vLLM, which manage the KV cache as a form of virtual memory.

question: According to the optimization lecture, how large is the KV cache for Llama-3-8B and Llama-3-70B at long context lengths?
reference_answer: The lecture gives a worked size formula: for Llama-3-8B at 32K context (FP16, batch=1), the KV cache is about 2 x 32 layers x 8 KV heads (with GQA) x 128 head_dim x 32768 x 2 bytes ~= 4.29 GB per request. For Llama-3-70B (80 layers, same 8 KV heads) at 32K context it grows to roughly 10.7 GB, and at 128K context to about 43 GB per request -- multiplied by batch size for concurrent users. The material adds that an H100 has 80GB of VRAM, Llama-3-70B FP16 weights need roughly 140GB (so at least 2 H100s just for the weights), and even 2 H100s leave too little headroom for a single 128K-context FP16 KV cache (~40GB at batch=1).
notes: Near-verbatim numeric grounding (4.29GB / 10.7GB / 43GB / 80GB / 140GB / ~40GB figures) in the 'Size Formula' section of 02_optimization.html; verified by direct chunk_id lookup. These are figures stated BY the lecture material, not independently fact-checked by us.

question: What problem does PagedAttention solve, according to the optimization lecture material?
reference_answer: The material explains that FlashAttention solved attention efficiency on a per-request basis, while PagedAttention solves the harder problem of fitting many different requests' KV caches into memory simultaneously when each grows to a different size -- managing the KV cache as a form of virtual memory (the basis of systems like vLLM).
expected_sources: 02_optimization.html, section 4 PagedAttention & vLLM: KV Cache as Virtual Memory
notes: Near-verbatim grounding in section 4 of 02_optimization.html; verified by direct chunk_id lookup.
